title: The Five-Formed Body of the Proprium
reading:
When self-love organizes itself within the soul, it does not remain a single simple craving. It takes a body. That body is articulated according to the full structure of the natural mind turned in on itself, so that the proprium, when it has come into its strength, has within itself five forms at once and can move from one to another at will.

Its head is a strong love grown ravenous — the appetite that wants to consume what it surveys. Its wings are thoughts that mount upward as if to reach the height, the proprium's mimicry of spiritual ascent. Its feet are the lower cravings that move it along the ground. Its belly is the dark substrate where what has been claimed is digested and held. Its loins are sense-knowledges swimming in their own waters, the natural perceptions out of which it generates further demand. These are not five separate creatures; they are one self-loving formation showing five aspects, and the soul should recognize that whichever face of self-love presents itself at a given moment, the others are present in it also.

Because it holds all five at once, the proprium can change its mode of operation as the situation requires. When it wishes, it walks on its lower cravings; when it wishes, it flies on its rising thoughts; when it wishes, it goes down into the natural waters and moves among sense-perceptions; when it wishes, it crawls in the dark. The soul that is being deceived by it should not be surprised when the same self-love that yesterday flew today crawls. It is the same body taking another of its forms.

Three further things belong to it. First, it has its beasts — the particular lower affections that follow it as a host. Second, it has its myriads — the gathered multitude of disordered thoughts that come out of it whenever it speaks. Third, its body is hard. The teeth of its own beasts cannot pierce it; no weapon of natural truth, however foundational, can cut it through. This hardness is not a strength of life. It is the hardness of what was molded out of single-minded reflection turned wholly in upon itself — the unyielding density of a self-claiming that admits no other.

Three more things. At one moment the fire of self-love flares through the whole body and it is all flame; at another moment it goes cold as snow, withdrawing every warmth so that nothing reaches it. And when its lower affections present themselves before it, it searches their hearts thoroughly, knows what is in them, knows what stands in their faces, until it has seen the whole of what they bring — though when they turn away from it, what is in their hearts is hidden from it, for it sees only what stands before its claim.

Yet for all this articulation and hardness and intelligence, there is no life in it at all. What it calls its life is the bile that runs from its face — the bitterness of its own claiming, mistaken for vitality. And in its belly is a corruption that stands firm before it, the settled rot at the center of every state self-love has organized.

This is what the soul is contending with when the proprium has taken its full form: not a simple temptation, but an articulated body that can shift among its modes, that gathers its multitudes, that hardens itself against every natural truth, that flames and freezes by turn, that searches what comes near it — and that has no life of its own at all, only the bile of its claiming and a corruption at the core. Seeing this is the beginning of laying it off.
